title: Charlie Watts - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 113,033 (the rest is references). Charles Robert Watts, born 2 June 1941, University College Hospital, Bloomsbury, London; raised in Wembley and Kingsbury; died 24 August 2021, Royal Brompton Hospital, Chelsea, aged 80. Earliest records jazz 78s, Jelly Roll Morton and Charlie Parker; at about thirteen took the neck off a banjo and played its head on a stand as a snare; wanted to play like Chico Hamilton with Gerry Mulligan, 'with brushes'; a GBP 12 kit for Christmas 1955, practised along to jazz records; Harrow Art School to 1960; advertising day job. Alexis Korner invited him into Blues Incorporated in 1961; rejoined February 1962; agreed in January 1963 to join the Rolling Stones, first public appearance as a permanent member at the Ealing Jazz Club, 2 February 1963. 'Ode to a High Flying Bird', a cartoon tribute to Charlie Parker, December 1964. Married Shirley Ann Shepherd 14 October 1964. Rocket 88 with Ian Stewart (late 1970s, with Jack Bruce among others); the Charlie Watts Orchestra (1980s); the Quintet (Warm and Tender, 1993; Long Ago and Far Away, 1996); the Tentet (Watts at Scott's); the Charlie Watts/Jim Keltner Project; the ABC&D of Boogie Woogie (from 2009). Playing: 'restrained, highly song-oriented', little interest in solos; from around 1969 he left out the hi-hat eighths on beats 2 and 4, which gave the snare more prominence and eased his workload; from about 1968 to the mid-1970s he often delayed the snare slightly on 2 and 4 ('Monkey Man', 'Wild Horses'); he often accelerated over a song, especially 'Honky Tonk Women', less in the studio after the mid-1970s; unlike most bands, he followed Keith Richards (Kakutani: what 'makes the Stones impossible to copy'). Kits: Ludwig in the 1960s; a Gretsch round badge in Black Nitron from 1968; from 1978 a late-1950s Gretsch round badge in natural maple, 22-inch bass drum, 12x8 rack tom on a separate stand, 16-inch floor tom, snare, hi-hat and four cymbals. The mid-1980s story of his punching Jagger for calling him 'my drummer'. Steve Jordan reported in August 2021 to take his place on the No Filter tour after heart surgery. Christgau: 'rock's greatest drummer'; Rob Sheffield: 'rock's ultimate drum god'; Jagger called him 'the Wembley Whammer'. Rock and Roll Hall of Fame 1989 (with the Stones), Modern Drummer Hall of Fame 2006, Rolling Stone's 100 Greatest Drummers No. 12 (2016); the Telegraph's best-dressed lists and Vanity Fair's International Best Dressed Hall of Fame (2006). Drummers who paid tribute include Roger Taylor (Duran Duran), Nick Mason, Questlove, Chad Smith, Max Weinberg and Peter Criss.

title: Rick Mattingly, 'In Memoriam: Charlie Watts', Percussive Arts Society
notes: Undated memorial quoting Mattingly's own interviews with Watts and with Keith Richards (1989). Watts: 'My thing is to make it a dance sound; it should swing and bounce.' 'I don't like drum solos ... generally I prefer drummers playing with the band.' 'My love was rhythm brushes - wire brushes. The first thing I heard that I wanted to emulate was Chico Hamilton playing brushes on "Walkin' Shoes" by Gerry Mulligan.' On the hi-hat: 'I was never conscious of doing it until Jim Keltner mentioned it. But I do it a lot. It really comes, I think, from coming down heavy on the backbeat. I suppose I got in the habit of pulling the stick out of the way to get a louder sound.' On grip: matched grip 'that Ringo uses' he played 'for a few years, because I thought it was popular'; Ian Stewart 'virtually ordered me to go back to what he called the "proper" way of playing. So I went back to the military grip, and I really do prefer it.' Richards: 'Whereas with Charlie, you suddenly realize that you're floating a few inches off the ground'; Watts with a click: 'Now, what it should do is come up a little bit in tempo here, and then it should pull back there'; 'That's what Charlie knows innately, and that's why I love him.' A simple four-piece kit throughout, usually a Gretsch, as the 1950s and 1960s jazz drummers he admired played; one of the few rock drummers who used brushes for certain songs. The Charlie Watts Jim Keltner Project (2000) has tributes to Art Blakey, Kenny Clarke, Tony Williams, Max Roach, Elvin Jones and others.

title: Eric Deggans, 'Appreciating Charlie Watts, The Rolling Stones' Understated Drum Master', NPR (via WBGO), 25 August 2021
notes: 'The epitome of a drummer who played for the band and for the song'; he often did not hit the hi-hat and the snare together on the backbeat, which he did not notice until Jim Keltner pointed it out. Honky Tonk Women: the snare lick 'almost seems to trip over the opening cowbell' before the beat settles; Start Me Up: 'an extra bass drum note' makes the guitar feel off-kilter before the beat comes in; Sympathy for the Devil: a cross-stick on a snare with the snares off beside the congas; Rock and a Hard Place (1989): upside-down china cymbals. He insisted Richards's amp be placed where he could hear it. Richards called him the band's 'hidden hero'. Watts (Later, 1993): 'The very nature of playing drums is a nervous twitch, really.'

title: Mikal Gilmore, interview with Charlie Watts (2013), published by Rolling Stone (Australia), 26 August 2021
notes: Previously unpublished. On drummers: Earl Phillips (Jimmy Reed's) 'kind of played like a jazz drummer'; Earl Palmer saw himself as a jazz player; Zigaboo Modeliste 'could play bebop but also could play second-line rhythms'; Ed Blackwell 'a revolutionary drummer with Ornette Coleman's quartet'; Sonny Greer with Ellington; 'If any young person asked me who they should follow in one's life, I'd say Roy Haynes'; Tony Williams 'an extension of Roy'; Keith Moon 'didn't play real time or anything' but was 'on top of everything'; 'I'm not Buddy Rich'. On himself: 'I've never had that virtuosity'; 'The drummer is the engine'; Keith is 'very much like playing with a jazz guy, very loose'; Richards's amp sits by his hi-hat; the Stones 'are the only people I want to play rock & roll with'.

title: Blues Incorporated - Wikipedia
notes: Founded by Alexis Korner and Cyril Davies, 1961; the 1961 line-up with Charlie Watts on drums, Jack Bruce on bass and Dick Heckstall-Smith on saxophone; the Ealing Club's Rhythm and Blues Night from 17 March 1962. When Watts left for the Rolling Stones he 'suggested Ginger Baker as his replacement'.

title: Tony Chapman - Wikipedia
notes: Read through a search summary only. Chapman, the Rolling Stones' drummer in 1962, 'felt that he did not fit in with the way-out approach of the group, and Charlie Watts took over as their permanent drummer' (January 1963).

title: Tumbling Dice - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 151,229. Basic track 3 August 1971 in Nellcôte's basement on the Rolling Stones Mobile, Mick Taylor on bass; finished at Sunset Sound, November 1971 to March 1972. Watts overdubbed a second drum track over the first, the only Stones song where he did; Jimmy Miller is credited with drums on the coda, acknowledged forty years later, because Watts was having trouble with it. At the start of each chorus the piano, bass and drums drop out. Sisario: Watts's backbeat gives it a 'languid strut'; Al Shipley: 'a perfect Charlie Watts snare fill'; Janovitz: a 'perfect tempo', a slight drag and a shuffle; Strummer: 'not a straightforward tempo'.
